title: Leaving Parliament: what worked, what still hurts
label: 15 September 2026 · General Election Planning
summary: Former MPs who lost their seats said the practical support after the 2024 election — from the House staff and IPSA (the independent body that handles MPs’ pay, pensions and expenses) — was much better than in the past and largely did its job. But they warned leaving Parliament is often a traumatic, very public shock, and staff were less well supported: rules about notice and pay were unclear, email access and device disposal felt harsh, and more career retraining and emotional help are needed.

speakers.label: Sir Charles Walker
speakers.name: Sir Charles Walker
speakers.role: Former MP for Broxbourne (2005–2024); former Chair of the Administration Committee

speakers.label: Baroness Debbonaire
speakers.name: Baroness Debbonaire
speakers.role: Thangam Debbonaire, former MP for Bristol West (2015–2024)

chapters.title: Overall view: support improved but not perfect
chapters.takeaway: House staff and IPSA largely delivered an improved package after 2024, but support still needs strengthening.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome. We’re asking former MPs about how well the support after the 2024 election worked when people left Parliament. Could you introduce yourselves?

turns.speaker: Nigel Mills
turns.text: I’m Nigel Mills, MP for Amber Valley from 2010 to 2024.

turns.speaker: Sir Charles Walker
turns.text: Charles Walker here, Broxbourne MP 2005–2024. I chaired the previous Administration Committee work on leaving Parliament, called “Smoothing the cliff edge.”

turns.speaker: Baroness Debbonaire
turns.text: Thangam Debbonaire, Bristol West 2015–2024.

turns.speaker: Mr Nigel Evans
turns.text: Mr Nigel Evans—former MP, served 32 years.

turns.speaker: Sir Charles Walker
turns.text: Short answer: the House service and IPSA did well after 2024. I can’t give 10/10 but I’d give about nine and a half out of 10.

chapters.title: The shock of losing: it’s public and traumatic
chapters.takeaway: Leaving suddenly is often experienced as trauma, especially when it happens in public and when staff must be made redundant.

turns.speaker: Bambos Charalambous
turns.text: How prepared were you for leaving, and what surprised you?

turns.speaker: Nigel Mills
turns.text: I’d seen the polls and expected it, but you can’t prepare fully. You can’t look for jobs in an active campaign, so the reality hits hard on the day you lose.

turns.speaker: Baroness Debbonaire
turns.text: Losing your job publicly is a form of trauma. You’re 58, unemployed on TV, and have to make staff redundant—there’s no real way to prepare for that public humiliation.

turns.speaker: Mr Nigel Evans
turns.text: I was genuinely surprised when my once-rock-solid seat fell. I’d never planned ahead. The practical help I was offered afterwards was, fortunately, good.

turns.speaker: Sir Charles Walker
turns.text: People should act as if their last day here might come even on their first day—this is a vocation with an expiry date for most, and the House should give better accredited retraining.

chapters.title: Staff, notice periods and redundancy: the weakest point
chapters.takeaway: Staff were often less protected than MPs—guidance on notice, pay and help into new jobs was unclear and inconsistent.

turns.speaker: Mary Glindon
turns.text: How realistic were the deadlines for winding up and how were your staff supported?

turns.speaker: Baroness Debbonaire
turns.text: A three-month winding-up period helped, but staff support was the main worry. My team planned secretly and found jobs quickly, but not everyone could, and the emotional impact was huge.

turns.speaker: Nigel Mills
turns.text: There was confusion about the four-month period people expected. Some staff assumed it meant four months’ pay—some MPs thought it was a cap, others a limit. That needs clarity.

turns.speaker: Mr Nigel Evans
turns.text: MPs got a cushion, staff didn’t. Many staff are young with mortgages and families; their position can be brutal. They should get the same protections as MPs.

turns.speaker: Nigel Mills
turns.text: The redundancy process felt odd: consultation meetings, a week’s notice, then an appointment a week later—it burns time and feels unhelpful when you already know there's no job.

turns.speaker: Sir Charles Walker
turns.text: If the House wants to be a serious employer it should fund ongoing professional development, with qualifications recognised by top universities or training bodies.

chapters.title: Practical problems: kit, email and handovers
chapters.takeaway: Practical help mostly worked, but device disposal, loss of parliamentary email, and casework handover caused distress and inefficiency.

turns.speaker: Kirsteen Sullivan
turns.text: Was the guidance from the House, IPSA and parties clear on what to do during Dissolution and winding up?

turns.speaker: Baroness Debbonaire
turns.text: Guidance was mostly good, but managers wanted a clear toolkit—how to destroy or keep data, recycle computers, and whether staff can finish casework during Dissolution.

turns.speaker: Sir Charles Walker
turns.text: I was upset to see old kit hauled off to a skip. Letting departing MPs buy useful kit or re-use it would avoid waste and avoid humiliating moments.

turns.speaker: Mr Nigel Evans
turns.text: Losing your parliamentary email is brutal. One simple idea: provide a standard ex-MP email address (like name.exmp@parliament.uk) so people know how to contact you afterwards.

turns.speaker: Marie Goldman
turns.text: Did casework handover to incoming MPs work?

turns.speaker: Nigel Mills
turns.text: Most casework dries up during a campaign. We offered to transfer files where constituents consented, but there weren’t many outstanding cases.

turns.speaker: Baroness Debbonaire
turns.text: Incoming winners often expect inherited urgent cases, but usually those are already handled. It’s sensible to assume new MPs will start from scratch unless there’s an exception.

turns.speaker: Nigel Mills
turns.text: One more practical point: references. IPSA will confirm employment dates, but if an employer wants more detail they email your personal address, which is awkward once your parliamentary email is gone.

chapters.title: Aftercare: careers support and emotional help
chapters.takeaway: Career transition coaching and private therapy were very helpful; the House should consider offering more emotional support and accredited retraining, and extending career help to staff.

turns.speaker: Bambos Charalambous
turns.text: Would you use the careers transition service and how important was emotional support?

turns.speaker: Baroness Debbonaire
turns.text: I used the careers service and it was invaluable for translating MP skills into jobs. I also paid for private therapy from February—therapy and careers coaching reinforced each other.

turns.speaker: Sir Charles Walker
turns.text: Outplacement and career coaching were useful. But we need accredited, serious retraining options and for MPs themselves to plan from day one for when they eventually leave.

turns.speaker: Nigel Mills
turns.text: Careers support should be offered to staff too. A good employer helps people into new roles; Parliament should be no different if it wants to recruit good staff.

turns.speaker: Mr Nigel Evans
turns.text: I still keep in touch with ex-staff. They deserve the same cushion and access to training as MPs if we want to attract top people to these jobs.

turns.speaker: Bob Blackman
turns.text: Would you come back to mentor new MPs?

turns.speaker: Sir Charles Walker
turns.text: No. New MPs don’t want defeated former MPs around. And many of us need paid work ourselves—most of us left and needed to find jobs, so unpaid mentoring isn’t realistic.

turns.speaker: Baroness Debbonaire
turns.text: I agree. New MPs should learn the job directly, and retired MPs aren’t the right free resource—people need to be paid for their labour and time.

chapters.title: What to fix next
chapters.takeaway: Keep the good bits (reception centre, careers coaching, clearer guidance), fix staff protections, clarify notice/pay rules, avoid wasteful disposal and provide email continuity and accredited retraining.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: To finish: what practical fixes would you recommend most strongly?

turns.speaker: Sir Charles Walker
turns.text: Develop accredited professional training for MPs, publicly funded career development, and make sure outplacement continues.

turns.speaker: Baroness Debbonaire
turns.text: Give clearer toolkits for office managers, better guidance on confidential waste, and make emotional support accessible—recommend private therapy to others who can afford it.

turns.speaker: Nigel Mills
turns.text: Clarify whether the four-month winding-up is a cap or a target, simplify redundancy paperwork and improve support for staff getting CVs and interview practice.

turns.speaker: Mr Nigel Evans
turns.text: Provide a straightforward ex-MP contact address so constituents and other organisations can still reach former MPs, and treat staff as equally deserving of cushioning.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all for clear, practical feedback. That concludes this session.
